title: AutoScaling_MultiAZ_Recovery
description: A PowerPoint Presentation about Auto-Scaling and Multi-AZ Recovery on AWS for high availability

sections.title: HIGH AVAILABILITY ON AWS
sections.subtitle: Slide 1 of 9 • PowerPoint Deck
sections.contentMarkdown:
* 
Recovery

* Keeping a virtual server running — and what happens to its data — when an entire availability zone goes down.

sections.title: THE BASICS
sections.subtitle: Slide 2 of 9 • PowerPoint Deck
sections.contentMarkdown:
* What Auto-Scaling Does
* Multiple subnets
* Auto-scaling can start EC2 instances across several subnets, not just one.
* Automatic failover
* If an entire availability zone has an outage, a new virtual server can be launched into another subnet in another zone.
* Continuous monitoring
* Auto-scaling watches the health of running servers and reacts when something goes wrong.
* AUTO-SCALING & MULTI-AZ RECOVERY
* 2

sections.title: SETTING IT UP
sections.subtitle: Slide 3 of 9 • PowerPoint Deck
sections.contentMarkdown:
* Launch Configuration
* Everything needed to launch a single virtual server:
* Image (AMI) to start the new server from
* Instance type — the size of the virtual server
* Auto-Scaling Group
* Tells EC2 how many servers to run and where:
* Min / max / desired number of virtual servers
* Health check for the virtual servers
* Subnets to launch virtual servers in
* AUTO-SCALING & MULTI-AZ RECOVERY

sections.title: TWO DIFFERENT RECOVERY MECHANISMS
sections.subtitle: Slide 5 of 9 • PowerPoint Deck
sections.contentMarkdown:
* CloudWatch Alarm Recovery
* Launches an identical copy of the original virtual server if it fails — but only in the same availability zone.
* Why only the same zone?
* The private IP address and the EBS volume of a virtual server are bound to a single subnet and a single availability zone.
* Auto-Scaling Failover
* Can recover a failed virtual server into a completely different availability zone — true protection against a data center outage.
* Example: a Jenkins CI server
* If a team relies on Jenkins to test, build, and deploy software, auto-scaling lets it fail over into another zone instead of staying down during a data center outage.
* AUTO-SCALING & MULTI-AZ RECOVERY

sections.subtitle: Slide 6 of 9 • PowerPoint Deck
sections.contentMarkdown:

sections.title: FIXING THE PITFALL
sections.subtitle: Slide 7 of 9 • PowerPoint Deck
sections.contentMarkdown:
* Three Ways to Recover Your Data
* 1
* Use a multi-AZ managed service
* 2
* Use EBS snapshots
* Snapshot your EBS volumes and restore from the snapshot when a server recovers in another zone. Snapshots are stored on S3, so they're available across zones.
* 3
* Use distributed third-party storage
* Tools like GlusterFS, DRBD, or MongoDB replicate data across zones themselves — powerful, but adds real operational complexity.
* AUTO-SCALING & MULTI-AZ RECOVERY
* 7

sections.title: WORKED EXAMPLE
sections.subtitle: Slide 8 of 9 • PowerPoint Deck
sections.contentMarkdown:
* Choosing a Recovery Strategy for Jenkins
* 1
* The constraint
* 2
* Why plain EBS isn't enough
* An EBS volume only exists in a single availability zone, which is exactly the problem being solved — so it can't be the whole answer.
* 3
* Why skip distributed storage
* GlusterFS, DRBD, and similar tools would work, but they introduce a level of operational complexity that isn't justified here.
* 4
* The chosen solution: EBS snapshots
* Recover the virtual server in another availability zone using an EBS snapshot. You only lose the data written since the last snapshot — not the entire volume.
* AUTO-SCALING & MULTI-AZ RECOVERY
* 8

sections.title: KEY TAKEAWAYS
sections.subtitle: Slide 9 of 9 • PowerPoint Deck
sections.contentMarkdown:
* Auto-scaling needs two pieces: a launch configuration (what to launch) and an auto-scaling group (how many, where, and how to monitor).
* A CloudWatch alarm can only recover a server in the same availability zone; auto-scaling can fail it over into a different zone entirely.
* EBS volumes are bound to a single availability zone — they don't automatically follow a server that recovers elsewhere.
* Fix that gap with a multi-AZ managed service, EBS snapshots, or distributed third-party storage — pick based on what your app actually needs.
* For disk-based apps like Jenkins, EBS snapshots hit the sweet spot: real recovery, without the complexity of distributed storage.
* AUTO-SCALING & MULTI-AZ RECOVERY
